quote: Beweisen dass zwischen $n$ und $n+a$ stets eine Zahl liegt, die {+x+} durch keine der Zahlen $1, 2, \dots$ $a$ theilbar ist oder die zu $a!$ primen Zahlen bilden keine stärkere Lücke als $a$ (am Anfange)
english: To prove that between n and n+a there always lies a number that is divisible by none of the numbers 1, 2, ..., a; or, equivalently, that the numbers prime to a! form no larger gap than a (at the beginning).
topic: The page notes Hurwitz's construction of a function that grows faster than every function in a given infinite sequence, then proposes proving that every interval from n to n+a contains a number coprime to 1,...,a, with a sketch using Chebyshev-type functions and an inversion formula.

triage.modern_statement: Let P(a) be the product of the primes up to a, so P(a) has the same prime factors as a!. An integer is divisible by none of 2..a exactly when it is coprime to P(a). Hilbert's claim is that every block of a consecutive integers contains a number coprime to a!. In other words, the gaps between consecutive integers coprime to a! are at most a. In modern terms this is a bound on Jacobsthal's function: j(P(a)) ≤ a, where j(n) is the smallest m such that every m consecutive integers include one coprime to n. Hilbert's parenthetical '(am Anfange)' may mean he only meant the gap at the start of the sequence (from 1 to the first prime above a). That weaker version follows from Bertrand's postulate, but the general claim is the Jacobsthal-function question.
triage.answered_by: The general claim is false. Small cases computed later show this. A Lean/Mathlib formalization verifies j(2310)=14 for 2310 = 2·3·5·7·11: after 113 the next number coprime to 2310 is 127. So the 13 integers 114–126 are each divisible by some number from 2 to 11, which contradicts the claim for a = 11. The general problem is now studied as Jacobsthal's function, introduced by E. Jacobsthal around 1960–61. Rankin gave lower bounds and Iwaniec gave the upper bound j(P(x)) ≪ x² (log x)². Further lower-bound work came from Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao (Annals 2016) in connection with large prime gaps. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Jacobsthal's function j(n) is the smallest m such that every sequence of m consecutive integers contains an integer coprime to n. For primorials it gives the maximal gap among integers coprime to them.

A formal Mathlib proof states jacobsthal 2310 = 14 for the primorial 2·3·5·7·11, with the bound attained: after 113 the next coprime number is 127. This gives a gap longer than a = 11, so the general claim fails.

j(P(x)) is the maximal gap between numbers free of primes ≤ x. The best known upper bound in this setting comes from Iwaniec's work on Jacobsthal's problem. The function is closely tied to large gaps between primes.
The lower bounds on Jacobsthal-type functions are due to Rankin, and upper bounds come from Brun's sieve and Iwaniec. Research continues, including a disproof of a conjecture of Jacobsthal.
Work on explicit and computational upper bounds for Jacobsthal's function h(k) continues (Costello & Watts).

triage.why: Hilbert's statement is exactly the claim j(P(a)) ≤ a for Jacobsthal's function at primorials. The verified value j(2310)=14 shows a gap longer than 11 among integers coprime to 11!, so the claim is false as stated in general. The real growth rate of j(P(x)) is still an open research topic, known only to lie between Rankin-type lower bounds and Iwaniec's roughly x² upper bound. It matters for work on large prime gaps (Ford–Green–Konyagin–Maynard–Tao). I found no source that links this specific note to Hilbert or that says how he meant '(am Anfange)'. If he only meant the first gap after 1, Bertrand's postulate settles it trivially. For those two reasons confidence is medium.
